# Depth Over Breadth: Designing Modules for the Next Reader

By Priya Okafor · https://example.com/essays/depth-over-breadth

Most advice about modules is about size. This essay argues that size is the wrong axis. What matters is how much a module asks of the people who call it, compared with how much it does for them.

## Deep modules

A deep module does a lot of work behind a small interface. The caller learns a handful of things and gets a great deal of behaviour in return. A file system is the classic example: open, read, write, close, and behind those four calls sit caching, scheduling, permissions, and recovery from crashes. Depth is a ratio, so a module can only be judged deep or shallow once you know what its interface is.

# Interface

An interface is a language keyword, as in Java or TypeScript, that declares a set of method signatures a class promises to implement.

It is like a job description: it lists the duties, and any candidate who can do them all can take the job.

`interface Shape { area(): number }` lets any class with an `area` method be passed where a `Shape` is expected.

updated: 2026-06-02

# Information Hiding

Information hiding is the practice of keeping a module's design decisions, such as its data layout or algorithm, inside the module, so callers cannot come to depend on them and the decisions can change without breaking anyone.

It is like a restaurant kitchen behind a pass: diners order from the menu and never see, or rely on, how the cooks organise the line.

A date library stores timestamps as nanoseconds internally but exposes only `before`, `after`, and `format`, so switching to microseconds later breaks no caller.

# Spaced Repetition

Spaced repetition is a review schedule that shows an item again just before you would forget it, with the gap growing after each successful recall.

It is like watering a plant less often as its roots deepen.

A card recalled correctly today returns in 3 days, then 8, then 20. A card missed returns tomorrow.

# Deep Module

A deep module does a lot of work behind a small interface. Its depth is a ratio: what it does for callers compared with what it asks them to learn. Here the interface means everything a caller must know to use it correctly, not just its method signatures. So you can only call a module deep or shallow once you know what its interface is.

It is like a car's pedals and steering wheel. You learn three controls, and behind them sit the engine, the gearbox, the brakes and the fuel injection, none of which you need to understand to drive.

A file system has four calls: `open`, `read`, `write` and `close`. Behind them sit caching, disk scheduling, permissions and crash recovery, and the caller sees none of it.

# Shallow Module

A shallow module asks callers to learn nearly as much as it does for them. Its interface costs about as much to understand as the work it saves, so using it gains you little over doing the work yourself. Being small does not make a module shallow, and being large does not make it deep.

It is like a receptionist who only forwards your call. You still have to know which department you need and what to say to them, and the receptionist has added one more step.

A `FileWrapper` class whose `openFile(path, mode)` just calls `open(path, mode)` is shallow. The caller still has to learn every mode and every error from the underlying call, and now has to learn the wrapper's name too.

Links: [[Deep Module]], [[Software Design]], [[Depth Over Breadth]]
